# Human-readable table formatting (avoid scientific notation in kable).
fmt_num <- function(x, digits = 3) {
  format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE, scientific = FALSE)
}
fmt_int <- function(x) format(as.integer(x), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)

The question

We have a Bayesian model of “healthy” gene expression built from a large single-cell atlas, and a small diseased cohort of our own — SAVI (STING-associated vasculopathy with onset in infancy), a handful of donors, sequenced as disease-associated monocytes, together with a matched CTRL group.

For a candidate biomarker gene we want to answer a deceptively simple question:

Is the gene’s expression in the SAVI cohort significantly different from what the healthy atlas says it should be?

The difficulty is that the two sides come from completely different statistical machinery: a Bayesian zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB) mixed model for the atlas, and a frequentist edgeR negative-binomial GLM for our cohort. To compare them we must (i) extract a quantity that means the same thing in both models, and (ii) make sure it is reported on the same scale. This report tells that story and documents the verification we did along the way.

The healthy baseline: a Bayesian ZINB atlas model

Each gene in the atlas is modelled with brms as a zero-inflated negative binomial regression on the raw counts, with a per-sample offset and a rich fixed/random-effect structure:

# (exposition only — the fit is reconstructed from a compressed store; see below)
formula <- bf(
  counts ~ 1 + offset(offset) +
    age_decade * sex + disease_groups_altered + ethnicity_groups + assay_groups_altered +
    (1 | dataset_id_altered) +
    (1 + age_decade * sex + ethnicity_groups | <finer grouping>),
  shape  ~ 1 + disease_groups_altered + assay_groups_altered + ethnicity_groups +
    (1 | tissue_groups)
)
brm(formula, data = data, family = zero_inflated_negbinomial())

The negative-binomial mean parameter for sample \(j\) is

\[ \log \mu_j \;=\; \underbrace{\text{offset}_j}_{\text{sequencing depth}} \;+\; \mathbf{x}_j^\top \boldsymbol\beta , \]

and the observed count is then \(y_j \sim \text{ZINB}(\mu_j, \phi, \pi)\), i.e. with probability \(\pi\) a structural zero and otherwise \(\text{NB}(\mu_j, \phi)\).

What the offset is

The offset is the log effective library size. In training it is defined from tidybulk::scale_abundance:

\[ \text{offset}_j \;=\; \log\!\frac{1}{\text{multiplier}_j}, \]

where multiplier\(_j\) is the TMMwsp scaling factor that maps sample \(j\) onto a chosen reference sample (the atlas column whose library size is closest to the mean). By construction the reference sample has multiplier \(=1\), so its offset is exactly 0. Everything the model reports “at offset 0” is therefore “at the reference sample’s depth”.

The universal (marginal) baseline

Our cohort’s metadata (age, sex, ethnicity, assay) is largely unknown. So instead of conditioning the baseline on specific covariates, we build a universal baseline: we hold the biologically required terms fixed (disease = Normal, tissue = blood, offset = 0), and marginalise over the unknown covariates by averaging the prediction over the full grid of their atlas levels. This yields, per gene, a large pool of posterior draws of \(\log\mu\) that represents “healthy expression across all plausible covariate combinations”.

What “μ” means — and why posterior_linpred, not posterior_epred

This is the first subtlety. For a zero-inflated NB model the two obvious brms extractors give different things:

extractor returns meaning
posterior_epred() \((1-\pi)\,\mu\) expected count (zero-inflation folded in)
posterior_linpred(transform = FALSE) \(\log\mu\) the NB location parameter (log scale)

We want the NB mean parameter \(\mu\) — the biological expression level before the zero-inflation machinery — because that is the quantity edgeR’s NB GLM also estimates. So the baseline draws are produced with posterior_linpred(transform = FALSE) and then exponentiated, not posterior_epred.

Code 
# How the baseline draws were generated (mu_test_epred_baseline.R).
log_mu_mat <- posterior_linpred(
  fit, newdata = nd_grid, transform = FALSE,   # log(mu), NOT epred
  re_formula = NULL, allow_new_levels = TRUE, sample_new_levels = "gaussian"
)
log_mu           <- as.numeric(log_mu_mat)   # pooled draws x grid (full spread)
grand_mean_draws <- rowMeans(log_mu_mat)     # per-draw average over the grid (see §[SE](#sec-se))

Baseline distributions on the log(μ) scale

Both baseline summaries live on the log(μ) scale because that is what posterior_linpred(transform = FALSE) returns — the NB location parameter before exponentiation. We expect both distributions to be approximately normal, for slightly different reasons:

  • Full marginal log(μ) draws (log_mu, pooled over posterior draws × covariate grid). Each draw is the linear predictor \(\log\mu = \text{offset} + \mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta + \text{random effects}\). That is a sum of many fixed and random components. Even though we marginalise over a discrete covariate grid (a mixture), the resulting cloud is bell-shaped: most mass sits near the typical healthy state, with heavier tails from rare covariate combinations (young vs senior, different ethnicities, etc.).

  • Grand-mean log(μ) draws (grand_mean_draws, one value per posterior draw). For each draw we average log(μ) over the full covariate grid. By the central limit theorem, averaging \(G\) grid points shrinks the variance by roughly \(1/G\) and pushes the distribution toward Normality much more tightly than the full marginal cloud. That is exactly why its SD (0.715) is less than half the full predictive SD (1.776): we are looking at uncertainty in the mean, not spread across conditions.

Code 
par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 2.5, 1))
dens_marg <- density(ep$log_mu, na.rm = TRUE)
dens_mean <- density(ep$grand_mean_draws, na.rm = TRUE)
ylim <- range(c(dens_marg$y, dens_mean$y))
plot(dens_marg, col = "#3b6ea5", lwd = 2, ylim = ylim,
     main = "Baseline log(μ): marginal vs grand mean",
     xlab = expression(log(mu)), ylab = "Density")
lines(dens_mean, col = "#e67e22", lwd = 2)
abline(v = ep$mean_log_mu, col = "#3b6ea5", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
abline(v = ep$mean_grand_mean, col = "#e67e22", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 1, 2, 2),
       col = c("#3b6ea5", "#e67e22", "#3b6ea5", "#e67e22"),
       legend = c("Marginal log(μ) (full spread)",
                  "Grand-mean log(μ) (grid collapsed)",
                  "Marginal mean", "Grand-mean mean"))

The cohort: an edgeR negative-binomial model

For our own samples we use the standard edgeR NB-GLM workflow, with a group-means design ~ 0 + group so that each group (SAVI, CTRL, reference) gets its own coefficient = \(\log\mu\) at offset 0, rather than a fold change relative to a reference.

The crucial alignment step: we set edgeR’s offset to the same scale_abundance definition the ZINB was trained with, anchored to the same reference sample. Then “offset 0” means the same thing on both sides.

Code 
se_test <- se_monocytic |>
  tidybulk::scale_abundance(method = "TMMwsp", reference_sample = ref_sample_name)

counts     <- assay(se_test, "counts")
meta       <- as.data.frame(colData(se_test))
offset_vec <- log(1 / meta$multiplier)                 # = training definition

group <- as.character(meta$Category); group[is.na(group)] <- "reference"
meta$group <- factor(group) |> fct_relevel("reference")

dge <- DGEList(counts = counts, samples = meta,
               genes = as.data.frame(rowData(se_test)))
reference <- which(colnames(dge$counts) == ref_sample_name)
dge$offset <- matrix(offset_vec, nrow(dge), ncol(dge), byrow = TRUE)

design <- model.matrix(~ 0 + group, data = meta)
colnames(design) <- sub("^group", "", colnames(design))

dge <- estimateDisp(dge, design)
fit <- glmQLFit(dge, design)
gi  <- match(gene_id, rownames(fit))

# Same dispersion mu_test.R uses (trended, falling back as needed).
nb_dispersion <- if (!is.null(dge$trended.dispersion)) {
  dge$trended.dispersion
} else if (!is.null(dge$tagwise.dispersion)) {
  dge$tagwise.dispersion
} else {
  rep_len(dge$common.dispersion, nrow(dge))
}
disp <- nb_dispersion[gi]

Are the two offsets the same thing?

Both models use exactly the same equation, \(\log\mu_j = \text{offset}_j + \mathbf{x}_j^\top\boldsymbol\beta\), with \(\mu\) on the raw count scale and \(\exp(\text{offset})\) the per-sample size factor. So conceptually the offset plays an identical role. But we should verify that edgeR’s normalisation and the training scale_abundance normalisation are the same numerically. We compared edgeR’s default offset (\(\log(\text{lib.size}\times\text{norm.factor})\) from calcNormFactors) against scale_abundance’s \(\log(1/\text{multiplier})\):

Code 
A <- DGEList(counts = counts, samples = meta)
A <- calcNormFactors(A, refColumn = reference, method = "TMMwsp")
off_calcNF  <- log(A$samples$lib.size * A$samples$norm.factors)   # edgeR default
off_scaleAb <- offset_vec                                         # scale_abundance

offset_check <- tibble::tibble(
  metric = c("correlation(off1, off2)",
             "off1 - off2 : mean (the global constant)",
             "off1 - off2 : SD (0 => perfectly parallel)"),
  value  = c(round(cor(off_calcNF, off_scaleAb), 6),
             round(mean(off_calcNF - off_scaleAb), 4),
             signif(sd(off_calcNF - off_scaleAb), 3))
)
kable(offset_check, caption = "The two offsets are identical up to a global constant.")
The two offsets are identical up to a global constant.
metric value
correlation(off1, off2) 1.0000
off1 - off2 : mean (the global constant) 15.1348
off1 - off2 : SD (0 => perfectly parallel) 0.0000
Code 
plot(off_scaleAb, off_calcNF, pch = 19, col = "#3b6ea5",
     xlab = "scale_abundance  log(1/multiplier)",
     ylab = "calcNormFactors  log(lib.size*nf)")
abline(a = mean(off_calcNF - off_scaleAb), b = 1, col = "#c0392b", lwd = 2)

Conclusion. The offset is the same quantity in the brms ZINB model and the edgeR NB model, and the two normalisation routines produce the same factors (correlation 1, differing only by a constant). We use scale_abundance solely because it re-anchors the reference sample to offset 0 — matching the brms training convention so that both sides report μ “at offset 0”.

The pitfall: edgeR’s coefficient is not μ at offset 0

It is tempting to read the cohort’s \(\log\mu\) straight off fit$coefficients[gene, group] (since offset 0 is the reference scale). This is wrong, and finding out why was the key discovery.

edgeR’s DGEList pipeline (glmFit/glmQLFit) internally rescales a supplied offset by a constant. As a result its coefficients are shifted on the absolute scale. The shift cancels in any group-vs-group contrast — edgeR’s intended use — so nobody normally notices. But we are comparing an absolute μ to an external baseline, where the shift does not cancel.

We verified the true NB mean three independent ways:

Code 
sav <- which(meta$group == "SAVI")
ctl <- which(meta$group == "CTRL")

nb_mle <- function(j) {
  # genuine NB MLE of log(mu) at offset 0, offset applied directly
  edgeR::mglmOneGroup(matrix(counts[gi, j], nrow = 1),
                      dispersion = disp, offset = offset_vec[j])
}
glm_nb <- function(j) {
  unname(coef(glm(counts[gi, j] ~ 1 + offset(offset_vec[j]),
                  family = MASS::negative.binomial(theta = 1/disp)))[1])
}

verify <- tibble::tibble(
  estimator = c("edgeR glmQLFit coefficient (the trap)",
                "edgeR mglmOneGroup (raw NB MLE)",
                "independent MASS::glm.nb"),
  SAVI_logmu = c(fit$coefficients[gi, "SAVI"], nb_mle(sav), glm_nb(sav)),
  SAVI_mu    = exp(c(fit$coefficients[gi, "SAVI"], nb_mle(sav), glm_nb(sav))),
  CTRL_logmu = c(fit$coefficients[gi, "CTRL"], nb_mle(ctl), glm_nb(ctl))
) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.x, 3)))
kable(verify, caption = "glmQLFit's coefficient is shifted by a constant (~0.85 here) for BOTH groups; the raw NB MLE is the correct μ at offset 0.")
glmQLFit’s coefficient is shifted by a constant (~0.85 here) for BOTH groups; the raw NB MLE is the correct μ at offset 0.
estimator SAVI_logmu SAVI_mu CTRL_logmu
edgeR glmQLFit coefficient (the trap) 6.392 596.976 4.657
edgeR mglmOneGroup (raw NB MLE) 7.262 1425.419 5.525
independent MASS::glm.nb 7.262 1425.413 5.525

The glmQLFit coefficient understates SAVI’s μ by a factor of roughly \(\exp(0.85)\approx 2.4\times\) — a constant shift visible in both groups (so it would vanish in a SAVI-vs-CTRL contrast, but it badly distorts the comparison to the healthy baseline).

Fix. Take the point estimate from the raw NB MLE (mglmOneGroup, offset applied directly), and use glmQLFit only for the QL-shrunk Wald SE, which is invariant to a constant offset shift. This is exactly what mu_test.R now does:

Code 
ql_se <- function(grp) {
  mu_all <- fit$fitted.values[gi, ]
  W      <- mu_all / (1 + disp * mu_all)              # NB IRLS working weights
  cov_un <- solve(t(fit$design) %*% (W * fit$design))
  sqrt(fit$s2.post[gi] * cov_un[grp, grp])
}

mu_comparison <- tibble::tribble(
  ~source, ~group, ~`log(μ)`, ~`μ @ offset 0`, ~`SE / spread`,
  "Baseline (marginal)", "Healthy atlas",
    ep$mean_log_mu, ep$median_mu, ep$sd_log_mu,
  "Baseline (grand mean)", "Healthy atlas",
    ep$mean_grand_mean, exp(ep$mean_grand_mean), ep$sd_grand_mean,
  "Cohort (edgeR NB MLE)", "SAVI",
    nb_mle(sav), exp(nb_mle(sav)), ql_se("SAVI"),
  "Cohort (edgeR NB MLE)", "CTRL",
    nb_mle(ctl), exp(nb_mle(ctl)), ql_se("CTRL")
) |>
  mutate(
    `log(μ)` = fmt_num(`log(μ)`, 3),
    `μ @ offset 0` = fmt_num(`μ @ offset 0`, 1),
    `SE / spread` = fmt_num(`SE / spread`, 3)
  )

kable(mu_comparison,
      caption = "Baseline vs cohort μ at offset 0 (reference scale). Baseline rows report the marginal mean/median and grand mean; cohort rows use the NB MLE point estimate + QL Wald SE.")

Standard errors on the log(μ) scale

The Welch test needs a standard error for each side. The code looks asymmetric — sd(grand_mean_draws) on the baseline vs a Fisher-information formula on the cohort — but both quantities answer the same question: how precisely do we know the mean log(μ) at offset 0? They are on equal footing in \(\text{SE}_{\text{diff}} = \sqrt{\text{SE}_1^2 + \text{SE}_2^2}\).

Baseline: posterior SD of the grand mean

For the biomarker test we use the grand-mean posterior, not the full marginal spread. Per posterior draw \(s\) we average \(\log\mu\) over the covariate grid (rowMeans on the draws × grid matrix), giving one scalar draw of the healthy mean \(\bar\ell_s\). The point estimate and its SE are:

\[ \hat\ell_{\text{base}} = \frac{1}{S}\sum_s \bar\ell_s, \qquad \text{SE}_{\text{base}} = \text{sd}(\bar\ell_1,\ldots,\bar\ell_S) = \texttt{sd\_grand\_mean}. \]

In Bayesian inference the posterior standard deviation of a parameter is its standard error — it already integrates every source of uncertainty the atlas model knows about (fixed-effect posteriors, hierarchical shrinkage, priors). There is no separate Fisher matrix to assemble because we hold the full posterior sample.

This is not the same as sd(log_mu) (the full marginal spread, ≈ 1.776). That larger SD mixes between-condition heterogeneity (young vs old, different ethnicities, etc.) with estimation noise. For a biomarker we compare to the average healthy μ, so the tighter grand-mean SD (≈ 0.715) is the correct null uncertainty.

Because each grand-mean draw averages \(G\) grid points, the distribution is also closer to Normal than the full marginal cloud (see the density plot above) — which makes the Gaussian Welch \(t\) a reasonable parametric companion to the rank test.

Cohort: QL Wald SE from glmQLFit

edgeR has no posterior draws. The cohort contributes a frequentist point estimate (mglmOneGroup, the raw NB MLE at offset 0) and a QL Wald SE reconstructed from the negative-binomial GLM curvature:

\[ \text{SE}_{\text{cohort}} = \sqrt{\hat\phi_g \;\bigl(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{W}\,\mathbf{X}\bigr)^{-1}_{kk}}, \]

where \(\hat\phi_g = \texttt{s2.post}\) is edgeR’s quasi-dispersion after empirical-Bayes shrinkage across genes, and \(\mathbf{W}\) is the diagonal matrix of NB IRLS working weights. For a log link and NB variance \(\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mu(1+\phi\mu)\),

\[ W_i = \frac{\mu_i}{1 + \phi\,\mu_i}. \]

With a group-means design ~ 0 + group, \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}\) is block-diagonal, so for cohort \(k\) with samples \(i \in k\) this collapses to the intuitive weighted “standard error of the group mean”:

\[ \text{SE}_{\text{cohort}}^2 = \frac{\hat\phi_g}{\sum_{i \in k} W_i}. \]

That is the NB/QL analogue of \(\sigma^2/n\) on the log scale — the same kind of object as sd_grand_mean, just assembled from the likelihood because frequentist GLMs do not carry a posterior.

Code 
# mu_test.R — QL Wald SE (invariant to a constant offset shift)
mu_all <- fit$fitted.values[gi, ]
W      <- mu_all / (1 + disp * mu_all)            # NB IRLS weights
cov_un <- solve(t(fit$design) %*% (W * fit$design))
se     <- sqrt(fit$s2.post[gi] * cov_un[cohort, cohort])

Why pair this SE with mglmOneGroup? The point estimate deliberately avoids fit$coefficients (§The pitfall), but the SE from glmQLFit is still valid: a constant additive shift of the offset reparameterises intercept ↔︎ offset without changing fitted \(\mu_i\), the design \(\mathbf{X}\), the weights \(W_i\), \(\hat\phi_g\), or \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta)\). Only the location of the coefficient moves; the Wald SE of the group mean does not.

Combining them in the Welch \(t\)-test

The deviation-from-mean Welch statistic is

\[ t = \frac{\hat\ell_{\text{base}} - \hat\ell_{\text{cohort}}} {\sqrt{\text{SE}_{\text{base}}^2 + \text{SE}_{\text{cohort}}^2}}, \]

with atlas and cohort treated as independent (different data). In code:

Code 
welch_t_from_mean_se(
  mean1 = mu_baseline$mean_grand_mean,
  se1   = mu_baseline$sd_grand_mean,    # posterior SD of the grand mean
  n1    = mu_baseline$n_grand,
  mean2 = cm$log_mu,
  se2   = cm$se,                        # QL Wald SE from glmQLFit
  n2    = cm$df + 1
)

Two implementation details matter:

  1. n1 = n_grand (large). The \(t\)-statistic uses se1 and se2 directly; n1 only feeds the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. Passing the (large) number of posterior draws tells the \(t\) distribution that the baseline component is effectively Normal — we do not want a fake small-sample inflation from Monte Carlo draw count when se1 already encodes that uncertainty.

  2. n2 = df.residual.adj + 1. The cohort side is genuinely small ($$5 SAVI donors), so the residual df from edgeR’s QL fit governs the \(t\) tail behaviour. In practice \(\text{SE}_{\text{cohort}}\) dominates \(\text{SE}_{\text{diff}}\), which is correct: precision is limited by the small cohort, not by the atlas.

The parametric Welch \(t\) is backed by a non-parametric check that makes no Gaussianity assumption on the baseline: mean(grand_mean_draws >= cohort_log_mu) ranks the cohort estimate directly in the posterior. The rank \(p\) is the robust primary; the Welch \(p\) is the parametric cross-check.

Baseline sd_grand_mean Cohort QL Wald SE
Paradigm Bayesian posterior SD Frequentist QL Wald SE
Estimand uncertainty in healthy mean log(μ) uncertainty in cohort mean log(μ)
Typical magnitude (TSC22D2) 0.715 0.257 (SAVI)
Dominates SE_diff? No (atlas is huge) Yes (few donors)

Bottom line. sd(grand_mean_draws) is not a shortcut — it is the complete Bayesian SE of the grand mean. The edgeR formula is the matching frequentist SE of the cohort group mean. Both refer to log(μ) at offset 0, both quantify uncertainty in the mean (not population spread), and they are combined appropriately in the Welch test.

The tests

Why we do not simply test predicted counts

The most direct-looking idea is: draw the baseline posterior-predictive counts (\(y^{\text{rep}}\)) and run a non-parametric (KS / rank) test of the observed cohort counts against them. We implemented this (bootstrapping_p_value), but it does not make much statistical sense as the primary test, for two reasons:

  1. It conflates three different sources of variation. A predicted count carries NB dispersion noise and the zero-inflation Bernoulli and the uncertainty in μ. Comparing a handful of observed counts to that mixture mostly measures sampling noise, not a shift in the underlying expression level.
  2. The cohort counts live on a depth that varies 250× between donors (24k → 6.1M reads here), so the raw-count distribution is dominated by library size, not biology.

In other words, the predictive-count test answers “could these exact counts have been emitted by a healthy individual?”, which is almost always “yes” given ZINB’s enormous variance. The question we actually care about is about the mean parameter μ, so we test on the linpred (log μ) scale instead. That is the quantity both models share, and it is where the signal lives.

If you still want the predictive-count KS as a reference, the revised bootstrapping_p_value builds the reference set deterministically: it maps each observed order statistic to the closest baseline quantile position \((i-0.5)/n\), rather than drawing a random baseline subsample. That removes unnecessary Monte-Carlo noise from the focal comparison while keeping the same bootstrap null calibration (KS(focal_draws, resampled baseline)).

Testing on the μ scale

We summarise the cohort as \((\log\hat\mu,\ \text{SE})\) and compare it to the baseline grand-mean posterior with a Welch \(t\)-test, plus a non-parametric empirical upper-tail rank (“what fraction of healthy grand-mean draws exceed the cohort?”). The two standard errors — posterior sd(grand_mean_draws) vs edgeR’s QL Wald SE — are derived differently but refer to the same estimand; see §Standard errors for the full justification.

Code 
welch_t <- function(mean1, se1, n1, mean2, se2, n2) {
  sd1 <- se1 * sqrt(n1); sd2 <- se2 * sqrt(n2)
  se_diff <- sqrt(se1^2 + se2^2)
  t_stat  <- (mean1 - mean2) / se_diff
  df <- (sd1^2/n1 + sd2^2/n2)^2 /
        ((sd1^2/n1)^2/(n1-1) + (sd2^2/n2)^2/(n2-1))
  c(t = t_stat, df = df, p = 2 * pt(abs(t_stat), df, lower.tail = FALSE))
}

Prediction interval vs deviation-from-the-mean — why the grand mean works

Here is the conceptual crux. The universal baseline’s spread is huge (SD of \(\log\mu \approx\) 1.78). But that spread is not uncertainty about the healthy mean — it is the biological heterogeneity between covariate conditions (a prediction interval). Two very different nulls follow:

  • Prediction interval (conservative). Use the full marginal spread as the reference. This asks “is the cohort outside the entire cloud of every plausible healthy condition?” — a very high bar. A genuine biomarker can be clearly elevated above the typical healthy cell yet still sit inside that giant cloud.

  • Deviation from the mean (lever a — the biomarker question). Collapse the covariate grid per posterior draw (rowMeans of the draws × grid matrix) to get the posterior of the healthy grand mean. Its SD (\(\approx\) 0.72) is the uncertainty in the mean (a credible interval), not the between-condition spread. This asks “is the cohort’s mean shifted from the average healthy μ?” — which is what a biomarker claim actually means.

Decomposing the variance is the whole trick: the grand-mean SD is less than half the full predictive SD, so the deviation-from-mean null is far tighter and has real power, without changing any data — only the estimand.

Code 
run_cohort <- function(grp, j) {
  cm_logmu <- nb_mle(j); cm_se <- ql_se(grp); cm_n <- length(j)

  # PREDICTION INTERVAL: vs full marginal spread
  w_pred <- welch_t(ep$mean_log_mu, ep$sd_log_mu, ep$n_draws, cm_logmu, cm_se, cm_n)
  rank_pred <- mean(ep$log_mu >= cm_logmu)

  # DEVIATION FROM MEAN: vs posterior of the grand mean
  w_mean <- welch_t(ep$mean_grand_mean, ep$sd_grand_mean, ep$n_grand, cm_logmu, cm_se, cm_n)
  rank_mean_up <- mean(ep$grand_mean_draws >= cm_logmu)

  tibble::tibble(
    group = grp,
    `PI Welch p`        = round(w_pred["p"], 4),
    `PI rank P(>=)`     = round(rank_pred, 4),
    `Mean Welch p`      = round(w_mean["p"], 4),
    `Mean rank P(>=)`   = round(rank_mean_up, 4)
  )
}
results <- bind_rows(run_cohort("SAVI", sav), run_cohort("CTRL", ctl))
kable(results, caption = "Prediction-interval (PI, conservative) vs deviation-from-mean tests. The latter is the biomarker-appropriate null.")

Final results

Code 
cohort_numeric <- tibble::tibble(
  group = c("SAVI", "CTRL"),
  log_mu = c(nb_mle(sav), nb_mle(ctl)),
  mu = exp(c(nb_mle(sav), nb_mle(ctl))),
  se = c(ql_se("SAVI"), ql_se("CTRL"))
)

final <- tibble::tribble(
  ~source, ~group, ~`log(μ)`, ~`μ @ offset 0`, ~`SE / spread`,
  "Baseline (marginal)", "Healthy atlas",
    ep$mean_log_mu, ep$median_mu, ep$sd_log_mu,
  "Baseline (grand mean)", "Healthy atlas",
    ep$mean_grand_mean, exp(ep$mean_grand_mean), ep$sd_grand_mean
) |>
  bind_rows(
    cohort_numeric |>
      transmute(
        source = "Cohort (edgeR NB MLE)",
        group,
        `log(μ)` = log_mu,
        `μ @ offset 0` = mu,
        `SE / spread` = se
      ) |>
      left_join(results, by = "group")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    `log(μ)` = fmt_num(`log(μ)`, 3),
    `μ @ offset 0` = fmt_num(`μ @ offset 0`, 1),
    `SE / spread` = fmt_num(`SE / spread`, 3),
    across(c(`PI Welch p`, `PI rank P(>=)`, `Mean Welch p`, `Mean rank P(>=)`),
           ~ifelse(is.na(.x), "—", fmt_num(.x, 4)))
  )

Reading the table:

  • SAVI sits at μ ≈ 1425 vs a healthy median of ≈ 160 — roughly a 8.9× elevation. Under the deviation-from-mean null it is significant (both the Welch \(t\) and the non-parametric rank reach \(p \lesssim 0.01\)), while under the ultra-conservative prediction-interval null it is not — exactly the expected behaviour given the universal baseline’s heterogeneity.
  • CTRL stays non-significant under both nulls (\(p \approx 0.3\)–\(0.6\)). This is the essential sanity check: the tightened (grand-mean) null is not manufacturing significance — it correctly leaves the control null while lifting the diseased cohort.

The final story / solution

Putting it together, the working recipe is:

  1. Same estimand both sides. Compare the NB mean parameter μ (log scale). From brms use posterior_linpred(transform = FALSE) — not posterior_epred (which folds in zero-inflation). From edgeR use the NB group mean.
  2. Same scale both sides. Give edgeR the same scale_abundance offset the ZINB was trained with, anchored to the same reference sample, so “offset 0” is identical. The offset truly is the same object in both models (verified: the two normalisations are parallel, correlation 1).
  3. Read μ correctly. Do not use glmQLFit$coefficients for the absolute μ — edgeR rescales the offset internally and the coefficient is shifted by a constant. Use the raw NB MLE (mglmOneGroup) for the point estimate and glmQLFit only for the QL-shrunk SE (invariant to that constant shift).
  4. Match the SEs. Baseline sd(grand_mean_draws) is the Bayesian SE of the healthy mean; cohort sqrt(s2.post · (X'WX)^{-1}_{kk}) is the QL Wald SE of the group mean. Both quantify uncertainty in log(μ) at offset 0 and enter the Welch test on equal footing.
  5. Pick the right null. Test against the posterior of the healthy grand mean (deviation-from-mean), not the full marginal predictive spread. The former is the uncertainty in the mean (a credible interval) and answers the actual biomarker question; the latter is a between-condition prediction interval and is needlessly conservative.
  6. Test on μ, not on predicted counts. The predictive-count KS test is kept as a reference but is under-powered and ill-posed for this question, because a predicted count mixes NB dispersion + zero inflation + depth.

With this, the SAVI biomarker reaches clear significance (\(p \lesssim 0.01\)) while the control remains null — the result we expected biologically, obtained through a principled, non-parametric test on the shared mean parameter.

The next natural extension is to move from a single gene to a biomarker panel: aggregating the per-gene deviations across the signature (still non-parametrically) gives substantially more power than any single gene against a universal baseline.
